author: "Juan De La Torre"

Explore the output of `process_coastal_weights()` — distance to the nearest
NOAA CUSP shoreline feature and the derived weight applied to coastal exposure
indicators (SWI, storm surge). Weight decays linearly from 1 at the shoreline
to 0 at 50 km. Water supplies > 50 km from the coast receive `NA`.

I think this makes more sense than dividing the results from our exposure indicators
by distance to coast. Dividing by distance to coast introduces the possibility of
increasing the exposure value, and the changes to the values are basically unbounded.
My reasoning is that when we weight these data we want to use the exposure values 
that have been assigned to them as their "maximum potential" exposure for that
indicator and tweak that value down, but not up. I also think that this bounds 
the potential transformations to the exposure indicators in a way that makes
this weighting easier to use and interpret.

Here are some simple calculations to demonstrate these points.

Dividing by distance to coast makes those water supplies that are very
close to the coast explode in vulnerability.

$$
x = \text{exposure indicator value} \\
dist = \text{distance to coast} \\
\text{weighted exposure} = \frac{x}{dist} \\
x = 1 \\
dist = 0.01 \\
\text{weighted exposure} = \frac{1}{0.01} = 100
$$
Just because the site is very close to the coast does not mean that it's exposure
should get that much bigger after it is weighted.

Here is how this same example would look like with this weighting method:

$$
\text{weighted exposure} = x \times (\frac{max_{dist}-dist}{max_{dist}}) \\
\text{In this case } max_{dist} = 50\text{km (or 50000m)} \\
\text{Lets plug x and dist in} \\
\text{weighted exposure} = 1 \times (\frac{50 - 0.01}{50}) = 1 \times (0.998) = 0.998
$$
With this method the exposure value did get a little smaller, but that makes more
sense than it getting way bigger. Between 0.998 and 100 I think that 0.998 is better 
weighted. Now let's see an example with something like a water supply 10km away.

$$
\text{weighted exposure} = \frac{x}{dist} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1\\
\text{weighted exposure} = x \times (\frac{max_{dist}-dist}{max_{dist}}) = 1 \times (\frac{50-10}{50}) = 0.8\\
$$
I think the point is clear, just wanted to expand on it since the original idea 
was to divide by distance to coast and I deviated from that.

# Setup

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r}
source("setup.R")
mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE)
```

# Load data

```{r}
parks <- getParkSystem()

park_centroids <- parks %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  st_transform(4326) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2], x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1])

water_supplies <- read_excel(
  here("data", "Water_Supply_Systems", "NPS_Water_Systems_Database_Joined.xlsx"),
  sheet = 1,
  na    = c("NA", "U"),
  skip  = 1
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    source_longitude = as.numeric(source_longitude),
    source_latitude  = as.numeric(source_latitude)
  ) %>%
  filter(!state %in% c("AK", "AS", "HI", "MP", "PR", "VI")) %>%
  left_join(
    park_centroids %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      dplyr::select(UNIT_CODE, x, y),
    by = c(park_unit = "UNIT_CODE")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    source_longitude = ifelse(is.na(source_longitude), x, source_longitude),
    source_latitude  = ifelse(is.na(source_latitude),  y, source_latitude)
  ) %>%
  filter(!str_detect(source_type, regex("municipal|hauled", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  drop_na(source_longitude, source_latitude) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("source_longitude", "source_latitude"),
           crs    = 4326,
           remove = FALSE)
```

```{r}
coastal_weights <- read_csv(
  here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "coast_comp", "coastal_weights.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
cusp <- st_read(
  here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data", "NOAA_CUSP", "cusp_shorelines.gpkg"),
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(5070)
```

```{r}
ws_mapped <- water_supplies %>%
  left_join(
    coastal_weights %>% select(-park_unit, -park_name),
    by = "wsd_source_id"
  )

# Find nearest point on CUSP shoreline for each coastal water supply
ws_coastal <- ws_mapped %>%
  filter(!is.na(coastal_weight)) %>%
  st_transform(5070)

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(ws_coastal, cusp)

nearest_lines <- st_nearest_points(ws_coastal, cusp[nearest_idx, ], pairwise = TRUE)

# Each LINESTRING has 2 endpoints: [1] water supply, [2] coast — extract coast points
coast_pts <- nearest_lines %>%
  st_cast("POINT") %>%
  .[seq(2, length(.), 2)] %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  st_transform(4326)
```

# Map

Color scales with `coastal_weight` — red means close to coast (weight near 1),
green means near the 50 km boundary (weight near 0). **Grey** points are
non-coastal (> 50 km from coast, `coastal_weight = NA`). **Black** points are
the nearest CUSP shoreline location to each coastal water supply.

```{r}
pal <- colorRampPalette(c("green", "yellow", "red"))

mapview(coast_pts,
        col.regions = "black",
        color       = "black",
        cex         = 3,
        layer.name  = "Nearest Coast Point") +
  mapview(ws_mapped,
          zcol        = "coastal_weight",
          col.regions = pal,
          na.color    = "grey",
          layer.name  = "Coastal Weight",
          popup       = leafpop::popupTable(
            sf::st_drop_geometry(ws_mapped) %>%
              select(wsd_source_id, park_name, shore_dist_m, coastal_weight)
          ))
```
